newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, North Korea to try to restart stalled talks.
newsitem.headline: Japan, North Korea to try to restart stalled talks.

text.p: Japan and North Korea announced on Friday they plan preparatory talks in the Chinese capital of Beijing next week to set a schedule for long-stalled negotiations aimed at normalising diplomatic ties.

"The two governments agreed earlier today to hold talks at the level of deputy director-general," Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a Tokyo news conference. North Korean media made a simultaneous announcement.

The August 21 talks at Japan's embassy in Beijing are aimed at establishing a schedule and agenda for formal normalisation talks, which have been stalled for nearly five years over acrimonious bilateral disputes, Ikeda said.

He declined to specify whether the agreement to meet in Beijing was tied to any conditions, like food aid, or whether Japan would raise allegations that North Korean agents kidnapped Japanese citizens in the 1970s and 1980s.
"All matters of mutual concern will likely be discussed in the context of establishing a programme for negotiations," Ikeda said. "There is no direct link between food aid and the talks."

He reiterated Tokyo's stance that it would decide whether to help North Korea based on "a review of various overall factors, including the United Nations emergency appeal". Bill Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said in Tokyo on Friday that North Korea's food crisis was getting worse and that Washington was likely to respond to any further appeals for food aid to North Korea.

The United States, a major food donor to North Korea, has provided $52 million this year through the U.N. World Food Programme to help stave off a famine caused by two years of disastrous floods compounded now by a drought.
Japan-North Korea normalisation talks have been stalled for five years over Japan's persistent demands that North Korea clear up the kidnapping allegations, which North Korea vehemently denies.

Tokyo has cited the abductions as the reason it refuses to join South Korea, the United States and international organisations in providing food aid to North Korea, where experts say the lives of millions of people are in danger.

Polls by mainstream Japan media show a slim majority of Japanese support humanitarian aid to their communist neighbour, although many harbour doubts this will reach the intended recipients, not North Korea's massive military.
Japan, which controlled Korea as a colony from 1910-45, normalised relations with South Korea in 1965 but has yet to establish diplomatic ties with North Korea.

Tokyo is likely to press Pyongyang for progress on allowing family reunion trips to Japan for the estimated 1,800 Japanese women who left for North Korea with their Korean husbands between 1959 and 1982.

Most of the Japanese women, whose Korean husbands are descendants of Koreans who were brought to Japan before World War Two, have not been heard from for years, and North Korea has not allowed the women to visit their families in Japan.
